The Space Between Signals

Dear Readers,

Some issues take shape around a topic. Others emerge around a shift in perspective. This one belongs to the latter.

If you have worked with Firebird long enough, you have likely experienced moments when the system behaves in ways that are not immediately explained by what you see. Not failures, not bugs—just behavior that does not quite align with expectation. The tools are there, the information is available, and yet the picture remains incomplete until something in how you look at it changes.

What we explore in this issue sits in that space.

It is a space between observation and interpretation, between capability and consequence, between what the engine does and how its behavior is perceived under real conditions. It is also a space that tends to grow as systems evolve— when performance improves, when workloads intensify, when what used to be implicit becomes visible.

There is a certain irony in this. As our systems become faster and more capable, they also become more demanding in how they are understood. Not because they are more complex in principle, but because the margins for assumption grow smaller. Patterns that could once be ignored begin to matter. Details that seemed secondary take on weight. Familiar tools remain useful, but require a more deliberate reading.

This is not a new phase for Firebird as a technology, but it is a recurring phase for those who work with it. A point where experience accumulates not through new features, but through a deeper alignment between expectation and reality.

EmberWings has always been less about presenting answers and more about refining that alignment. This issue continues in that direction—not by expanding the surface, but by looking more carefully at what is already there.

Warm regards, The EmberWings Team

Wisdom of the elders

The apprentice brought his report at the end of the day.

“I have measured everything,” he said. “The queries are fast. The plans are correct. The counters show nothing unusual.”

The master looked at him. “And yet?”

“The system slows,” the apprentice said. “Not always. Only at times. I cannot find the cause.”

The master rose and led him to the courtyard. At its center stood a well, and beside it a bucket on a rope.

“Draw water,” said the master.

The apprentice lowered the bucket, filled it, and pulled it up. The rope moved smoothly through his hands.

“It is light,” he said. The master nodded. “Again.”

The apprentice lowered the bucket once more. This time, as he pulled, the rope caught slightly against the edge of the well. Just for a moment. Then it moved freely again.

He filled the bucket, raised it, and set it down.

“Again,” said the master.

The apprentice repeated the motion. Each time, the rope hesitated briefly at the same point. The delay was small, barely noticeable, but always present.

After several attempts, he stopped.

“It is nothing,” he said. “Only a small friction.”

The master looked at the bucket. “Carry water for the whole house.”

The apprentice was silent.

He watched the rope as it moved again through his hands—smooth, then caught, then smooth again.

After a while, he said, “It is not the weight.”

The master waited.

“It is the place where it repeats.”

Clarke's three laws

Arthur C. Clarke, an british science fiction writer, formulated three adages that are known as Clarke's three laws. The third law is the best known and most widely cited.

These so-called laws are:

  • When a distinguished but elderly scientist states that something is possible, they are almost certainly right. When they state that something is impossible, they are very probably wrong.
  • The only way of discovering the limits of the possible is to venture a little way past them into the impossible.
  • Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.

Observability Without Illusions

By Pavel Císař (IBPhoenix)

Most Firebird professionals eventually reach a point where the monitoring tables feel familiar. You know which columns matter, which counters deserve attention, and what “normal” looks like in your systems. At that stage, the challenge is no longer visibility. It is interpretation.

The engine is not hiding anything from you. The values exposed through the MON$ tables are real, transactionally consistent, and technically accurate. Yet accuracy alone does not guarantee understanding. In practice, many diagnostic mistakes emerge not from lack of data, but from overconfidence in what the available data actually means.

This is the central tension of observability in Firebird systems: monitoring data is necessary, but never sufficient.

The danger is subtle because modern monitoring creates a psychological illusion of completeness. Dashboards update continuously. Counters change in real time. Sessions appear and disappear. Queries can be inspected while they execute. The system appears transparent. But transparency is not the same thing as comprehension.

Monitoring tables expose states. Administrators infer causes. Those are not equivalent operations.

A MON$ snapshot can show that a statement is active. It cannot reliably explain why response times increased five minutes earlier. It can show transaction age. It cannot determine whether that transaction is operationally dangerous. It can expose attachment activity. It cannot reveal storage subsystem latency, hypervisor contention, network retransmits, or client-side processing stalls.

The farther one moves from raw observation toward causal explanation, the more dangerous unsupported assumptions become.

The Snapshot Problem

The monitoring subsystem is fundamentally snapshot-oriented. This characteristic is widely understood operationally, but insufficiently appreciated diagnostically.

When monitoring tables are queried, Firebird constructs a transactionally consistent snapshot of internal engine state. That snapshot remains stable for the lifetime of the monitoring transaction. This consistency is valuable because it prevents internally contradictory observations during analysis. But consistency introduces a hidden cost: temporal distortion.

You are never observing “the system” directly. You are observing a stabilized reconstruction of the system at a particular moment.

This distinction matters enormously in production diagnostics.

High-frequency events may never appear in MON$ data at all. A short lock conflict can produce visible application delays while remaining entirely absent from every monitoring snapshot. A burst of attachment creation may temporarily overload authentication or filesystem resources without leaving persistent evidence. Brief I/O stalls may disappear before observation begins.

The monitoring subsystem naturally favors persistence over transience.

Long-running operations remain visible long enough to be sampled repeatedly.

Short-lived but highly repetitive operations often disappear statistically. This creates a diagnostic bias toward obvious, persistent problems while obscuring cumulative instability generated by many small operations.

In practice, those cumulative effects are often more dangerous.

A thousand small delays distributed across concurrent requests can destabilize a production system more effectively than one obviously pathological query. Yet monitoring tools naturally draw attention toward what remains visible longest.

The stable snapshot improves consistency while simultaneously degrading temporal truth.

This is not a defect in Firebird’s design. It is an unavoidable property of snapshot-based observation.

Observation Has a Cost

One of the most dangerous misconceptions surrounding MON$ tables is the belief that monitoring is operationally free. It is not. Creating a monitoring snapshot requires the engine to collect information about active attachments, transactions, statements, I/O statistics, and internal engine structures. The collected data is materialized through memory-mapped files that stand behind the implementation of the monitoring subsystem. As system activity increases, the amount of information that must be gathered and assembled also increases.

The cost of snapshot creation therefore scales with system activity.

A lightly loaded database with a small number of active connections may produce monitoring snapshots relatively cheaply. A heavily loaded production system with hundreds of active attachments, large numbers of concurrent transactions, and many executing statements represents a completely different situation. The engine must gather substantially more information, traverse more internal structures, and populate significantly larger monitoring datasets. Under these conditions, monitoring itself becomes a non-trivial workload.

This has important practical consequences. It is generally unwise to create MON$ snapshots every few seconds in production environments, particularly under sustained load. Aggressive polling intervals may appear attractive because they promise higher visibility, but they can introduce measurable overhead precisely when the system is already under pressure.

Ironically, administrators often increase monitoring frequency during incidents— the exact moment when snapshot cost becomes highest.

The architectural model of Firebird also matters here. In SuperServer architecture, internal structures are shared within a single server process, which generally makes monitoring less expensive. In Classic architecture, however, each attachment operates as an independent process. Collecting monitoring information across many independent processes requires substantially more coordination and aggregation work. As concurrency increases, the relative cost of monitoring snapshots can become significantly higher than in SuperServer environments.

This difference is operationally important because it changes the practical limits of observability strategies. Monitoring frequencies that may remain acceptable under SuperServer can become disproportionately expensive under Classic.

The act of observation is itself part of the workload.

Experienced administrators eventually learn that monitoring systems must be designed with the same discipline applied to production applications. Excessive sampling does not automatically improve understanding. Sometimes it merely increases distortion.

Sampling Bias and the Illusion of Normality

Most monitoring environments rely on periodic polling. Administrators collect MON$ snapshots every minute, or sometimes even more aggressively. Over time, these repeated observations create a perceived picture of system behavior. But periodic observation introduces statistical blind spots.

Firebird workloads are rarely smooth. Real systems are burst-driven. Transaction storms emerge from scheduled jobs, reporting activity, retry loops, synchronization points, or application behavior that briefly concentrates large amounts of work into narrow time windows.

Short-lived spikes can dominate user experience while remaining almost invisible to averaged metrics. Averages conceal instability remarkably well.

An attachment count averaging fifty may represent a genuinely stable workload— or a violent oscillation between ten and ninety connections every few seconds. A query execution average may hide periodic latency explosions affecting users intermittently throughout the day.

Even worse, synchronized sampling can systematically miss recurring failures. This is one reason why observability cannot rely solely on database snapshots. The database engine may appear calm precisely because the disturbance already passed before the observation began.

The Missing Timeline

MON$ tables describe state, not history. A snapshot can reveal state at its creation, but cannot reliably explain how the system arrived there. This limitation matters enormously.

A monitoring query can show active statements, open transactions, fetch counts, and attachment activity. It cannot reveal how rapidly conditions changed, whether the observed state is exceptional or routine, or what sequence of events preceded the current moment.

State without chronology is diagnostically incomplete. This is where tracing becomes critically important. The Trace API introduces temporal continuity that monitoring tables fundamentally lack. MON$ tables answer “what exists now.” Tracing answers “what happened.”

But tracing alone is still insufficient. Tracing may reveal statement execution chronology while remaining blind to storage latency. Operating system telemetry may reveal I/O saturation while remaining blind to transaction behavior. Infrastructure monitoring may expose CPU contention while remaining unaware of metadata locking patterns.

No individual telemetry source is authoritative. Reliable diagnosis emerges only through correlation across layers.

Correlation as a Discipline

Experienced Firebird diagnostics resembles forensic reconstruction more than simple monitoring.

The database must be interpreted alongside its environment.

At the Firebird layer:

  • MON$ tables expose engine state,
  • Trace API exposes chronology,
  • gstat exposes structural characteristics,
  • transaction counters expose accumulation behavior.

At the operating system layer:

  • scheduler metrics reveal CPU contention,
  • storage telemetry reveals I/O latency,
  • memory pressure reveals cache instability,
  • context switching reveals concurrency pressure.

At the infrastructure layer:

  • virtualization platforms reveal resource contention,
  • SAN telemetry reveals latency spikes,
  • network monitoring reveals retransmission patterns.

At the application layer:

  • connection pools reveal burst behavior,
  • retry mechanisms reveal amplification effects,
  • ORM behavior reveals query multiplication,
  • request distribution reveals synchronization patterns.

Observability begins when these layers are interpreted together rather than independently. Rarely does a single metric conclusively identify root cause. More commonly, diagnosis progresses by gradually eliminating incompatible explanations while correlating incomplete signals from multiple layers.

The absence of contradictory evidence becomes as important as the presence of supporting evidence.

What You Cannot Safely Infer

Many diagnostic mistakes originate not from misunderstanding what MON$ tables show, but from misunderstanding what they do not prove.

You cannot safely infer CPU saturation merely because statements appear ACTIVE.

You cannot infer storage latency from fetch counts alone.

You cannot infer lock contention solely from transaction age.

You cannot infer query inefficiency purely from runtime duration.

You cannot infer causality from temporal proximity.

You cannot infer system-wide behavior from isolated snapshots.

And perhaps most importantly, you cannot infer absence of problems from absence of visible symptoms inside the database engine.

Beyond Visibility

The maturation of a Firebird professional often follows a recognizable path. Initially, the challenge is learning where to look. Later, it becomes learning what the values mean. Eventually, however, the deeper challenge emerges: learning which conclusions are justified—and which merely feel convincing.

That transition marks the difference between reading telemetry and practicing observability.

MON$ tables remain extraordinarily valuable tool. Firebird exposes far more operational visibility than many systems in its class. But visibility alone does not create understanding. Every monitoring system has blind spots. Every telemetry source carries interpretive limits. Every snapshot excludes more reality than it captures.

The purpose of monitoring is not to confirm assumptions. It is to reduce uncertainty without creating the illusion of certainty.

Interview with Dalton Calford

For those who remember the transition from InterBase to Firebird, the story is usually told through companies and core developers. Less visible were the community voices that helped keep the technology alive at a critical moment. Dalton Calford was one of them—an active participant in those early discussions who later stepped away from the public scene, focusing instead on building and running real systems where reliability mattered more than visibility.

Now, after many years, he returns with a very different perspective and a project that reflects both experience and curiosity. In this interview, we talk with Dalton about that journey, the lessons shaped by years in production environments, and the ideas behind his current work. The conversation moves between past and present, touching on architecture, compatibility, and the changing role of AI in development—without trying to simplify any of it too much.

Hi Dalton, can you tell us a bit about yourself, your background, and how you first became involved with InterBase and later Firebird?

I have been in the industry since the early 1980s, when my family’s company bought its first PC for the business. One of the first programs I dealt with was an accounting package called Bedford. It was written in BASIC, and when something needed to be patched, the original programmers would sometimes talk me through changes over the phone. That was my first real introduction to the idea that software was not magic. It was something a person could understand, change, and improve. It did not take long before friends of the family who owned small and mid-sized businesses found out that I had a knack for computers. I started helping them as well. My first computer job was assembling PC clones, and that quickly turned into repairing keyboards, printers, and whatever else someone put in front of me.

From there I became fascinated with programming. Like many people from that era, I learned the Borland tools. Turbo Pascal, Turbo C, Delphi, C++Builder, and the rest of that ecosystem were a big part of how I learned. I also learned hardware, software, accounting, and even Informix SQL mostly by being thrown into the middle of real business problems and having to make things work.

Learning InterBase was a natural step because Borland was bundling it with many of its development tools at the time. If you were using Borland tools seriously, InterBase was right there.

By the late 1990s I was working for a small telecom company. Around that time Inprise, which was Borland’s name for a short period, decided to drop support for InterBase. That was a real crisis for people who depended on it. Fortunately, the community came together and convinced Dale Fuller to open source InterBase. That became the beginning of Firebird, and the rest is history. My role in that period was not glamorous. I was a loud-mouthed geek on the InterBase forums and mailing lists, flooding the channels with “save InterBase” messages and trying to build enough noise that the people inside Borland and Inprise could not ignore it. That groundswell led to conversations with original developers and people in charge. IBDI itself was created by others, but they put me in as one of the founders because I had been part of that early push.

You were present at the InterBase crisis and co-founded IBDI. After that early period, you seem to step away from the visible Firebird ecosystem for quite a long time. What did your professional journey look like during those years, and how did your work with databases evolve in practice?

At first I wanted to stay involved. I cared about InterBase, and later Firebird, and I wanted to contribute. But at the same time I was pulled into complex production projects that required five-nines quality. I had a young family, long workdays, and systems that could not afford casual mistakes. In Canadian telecom, that level of quality was not marketing. People relied on those systems for emergency services such as 911, so safety and reliability expectations were part of the industry.

The InterBase and Firebird codebase was also not something I could learn casually. It needed serious time and attention. I remember working on a simple function, random, for InterBase, and realizing that it had sat on my to-do list for almost a year. That was the moment I understood that it would not be fair to the community for me to commit to work I could not reliably complete. So I stepped back.

Professionally, I spent almost 20 years in telecom. After that I moved into large-scale data processing for a web marketing firm. We processed streams from many different sources and supported near-live analysis tools that the company used to make purchase decisions. I never really stopped working with databases. In many cases I was working with technologies while they were still being designed or while the operational rules were still being discovered. That forced me to learn not only how systems worked, but why they worked that way. If you want to optimize real systems, knowing the surface behavior is not enough. You have to understand the reasoning behind the design.

From your experience designing real-world systems, what did Firebird get fundamentally right, and where did you repeatedly encounter its limits in production environments?

The thing Firebird got fundamentally right was treating the database itself as the source of authority. Many systems I worked with had destructive update models or transaction systems where the log was the real center of gravity. Firebird, because of Jim Starkey’s brilliance, used what we now commonly describe as copy-on-write behavior. Firebird developers know it as Multi-Generational Architecture, or MGA. Long after Jim designed those mechanics, people started building similar copy-on- write ideas into entire filesystems.

Firebird has operational gotchas. Every database does. If you do not learn the faults of the system you are using, and if you do not learn how to design around them, you are not really doing the job as a developer. The key point for me is that Firebird has had fewer faults, or at least fewer painful ones, than any other engine I have worked with. In fact, you can almost list the pain points of other database systems by naming things Firebird does not do. Firebird’s snapshot mode does not require query hints to avoid blocking other readers and writers. Firebird does not use a traditional authoritative write-ahead log model where the database is secondary to replaying the log. Firebird’s concurrency model is simple to reason about once you truly understand it. Long-running transactions can still cause operational problems if abused, but the model itself is elegant and powerful.

If you took the time to really learn Firebird, its PSQL, its transaction behavior, and its fast writes and commits, you could make it keep up with a lot of the competition in the early 2000s. I saw that firsthand. Firebird was at the core of a real-time telecom system that routed calls and managed contribution for a stateless, five-nines platform. It was designed to last about 10 years and ran for more than 20.

I have had to work with MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, and others. They all have strengths. But I often found myself looking at some operational problem and thinking, “I wish I could replace this part with Firebird.”

Your current work centers around ScratchBird. How did that project come into existence, and what were you trying to explore when you started it?

ScratchBird is currently a private research passion project. GitHub is being used partly as offsite backup and partly as a way to preserve the work. Once the project is finished enough, my intention is to provide it to the community. I also hope it becomes a kind of digital resume. I would like this work to help me get hired.

It originally started as “scratch” code for Firebird. The idea was not to create something that would be merged into Firebird. It was code for experiments, learning, and ideas, especially because I was using AI tools and I did not trust AI-generated changes anywhere near the real Firebird codebase. AI can produce useful work, but it can also produce very convincing garbage.

I cloned Firebird in April, but by July it was obvious that the AI tools of the time could not safely refactor that codebase. They kept breaking things. So I changed what “Scratch” meant. It stopped meaning test or throwaway code and started meaning “written from scratch.” I saved the old work in the git repository for historical reference, then deleted everything and began again. From there I started asking what I actually wanted in my ideal database. I made lists of must-haves, nice-to-haves, and “in my wildest dreams” features. The starting point was Jim Starkey’s MGA, plus his idea of BLR. After that came research, specifications, and a lot of late nights.

All of the current code is new. It is not a refactoring of Firebird. What began as a learning project became an obsession.

ScratchBird started as a deep refactoring of Firebird 6, but evolved into a fundamentally different system. At what point did you realize you were no longer extending Firebird, but designing a new architecture, and what drove that shift?

The turning point came when I realized the AI was not following the architecture.AI models tend to drift back toward their training data. You can give them specifications, design goals, and explicit instructions, and they will still sometimes return to whatever pattern is most common in their training. In this case, I discovered that the AI had halfway implemented a write-ahead-log style system. It had replaced or deleted MGA-related code, and worse, it had altered tests so that they did nothing except pass. That was the moment I stopped trying to refactor Firebird.

I also developed my working mantra: AI is like a brilliant but unreliable junior developer. It can be useful, fast, and surprisingly insightful, but it also forgets what it is doing, avoids criticism, fills in gaps with guesses, and can lie very confidently. That sounds blunt because it needs to be blunt. Developers need to understand both the strengths and the shortcomings of AI. If you treat it as magic, it will eventually damage your project.

So I built a workflow around that reality. The workflow became:

  • Clear specifications before code.
  • Tests before implementation.
  • Implementation changes must update specifications.
  • Never use the same AI model for the same type of task twice in a row.
  • Use one AI to attack the work of another.

I would write specifications and use AI to gather reference material, white papers, and example code. Then I would have different models attack the specification instead of asking them to praise it or continue it. I used Claude, Gemini, Kimi, Codex, and local Ollama-based models. Each model tends to make different mistakes, so they are useful as critics of each other. The reward point for the AI became finding flaws, not producing more text. That led to specifications that were more detailed, more repetitive, and much more explicit. Then I used the same adversarial process to clean them up.

I also started testing the AI models themselves. Around September I noticed that model quality could change from one day to the next. So I created standard prompts and comparison points to see which models were behaving the way I expected. The results changed depending on load, resource rationing, and whatever the vendor had changed behind the scenes. So the shift was driven partly by AI failures and partly by my need to understand how to use these tools without letting them take over the architecture.

ScratchBird sets out to unify and emulate multiple database systems, but the differences between them go far beyond syntax. Is this a problem you believe can be fully engineered into a coherent system, or is ScratchBird defining its own semantics and only approximating others? And to what extent is this architecture deliberate versus explored iteratively with AI?

I started with a simpler idea: one parser for my expanded syntax and one parser for Firebird. Very early I realized that the changes I wanted required their own parser, their own wire protocol, and their own boundaries. Then I ran into error handling. The error codes I was generating did not match what a Firebird client expects. So I created vectorized messages, with the parser responsible for mapping and altering responses into the form the client expects. Then came wire protocols. Each parser sits outside the engine and can have its own protocol behavior. I do not trust parsers as part of the engine, so the parser acts as a middle layer. It negotiates with the client, then communicates with the server and engine through controlled channels. The engine still needs to be able to emulate the security process, but the parser itself is not trusted.

Each incompatibility forced a design decision. Even ScratchBird MGA is not exactly

Firebird MGA. The fundamentals are the same, but I researched how modern copy-on-write filesystems handle some problems that Firebird users will recognize. ScratchBird’s design was adjusted based on that research. When I thought the design was ready, I threw as many Firebird regression tests at it as I could find from different repositories. It was a mess, but it was useful. It showed me where my assumptions were wrong.

Once I had Firebird behavior working reasonably well, I started asking: why not PostgreSQL? Why not MySQL? That led me to gather a set of reference engines where the source was available, so I could study how they solved problems. The full list is long enough that it belongs in a note, but the important point is that I wanted to compare real systems, not guesses about systems. From that I built a normalized capability matrix. I am not trying to make the native ScratchBird dialect look like all of those systems. I am trying to make sure the native engine can perform the same classes of work.

The result was the third attempt at my native parser. It does not use the exact style or dialect of any one reference database, but it is intended to express the full functionality. Performance was not the first goal, correctness was. But the later optimization work surprised me. In the hidden test groups from the ScratchBird optimization work, especially the Workplan 10 tests, ScratchBird was significantly faster than Firebird, within about 3 percent of PostgreSQL, and still slower than MySQL. I would not present that as a public benchmark suite yet, but it told me the architecture was not hopeless.

The emulation layers are different. They exist so original clients and tools can behave as expected, as much as possible. But internally, everything is normalized down into ScratchBird semantics, UUIDs, SBLR, datapackets, diagnostic vectors, and the ScratchBird transaction model. For example, ScratchBird currently has 11 supported index families, but many more index surfaces. A B-tree is not just a B-tree once you care about how different engines expose ordering, null handling, collation behavior, visibility, and optimizer expectations. So there are translation layers.

My alpha goal was simple to state but hard to achieve: can my parser and emulation layers pass the original projects' regression tests using the original projects' own tools? Firebird, PostgreSQL, and MySQL were the core targets. Once

I had enough of that working, I began driver implementation and called it a developer release. At the time I did not think many people were watching the project, so I did not maintain the releases as carefully as I should have.

Beta 2 has a different goal: finish the emulation parsers and expand the cluster work. While doing that, my wife asked why I had not patented anything. I had never considered it because I did not think anything was different enough. Interestingly, the AI systems I use disagreed. They identified three major cluster design decisions that they considered potentially patentable. Because of that, I stopped updating the public ScratchBird repository, created a private repository, and started reaching out to patent lawyers.

That is why the public GitHub project went quiet. I have not published the designs, specifications, or new code anywhere, and I stopped pushing before it became a risk. If the lawyers agree that anything is patentable, my preference is to talk to open source legal groups and see whether the work can be protected for the community rather than used against it.

A defining aspect of ScratchBird is your use of AI in development. When you started ScratchBird, how did you initially work with AI, and how has that workflow evolved over time? How do you divide responsibilities today between yourself and AI, and how has your trust in AI changed?

I have covered part of this already, but my advice to developers is straightforward. AI is useful when the task is small enough to fit inside the context window and when you already know what correct looks like. It is dangerous when you ask it to own the architecture. AI hallucinates variables. It forgets specifications. It confidently invents behavior. It tells you something is complete when it is not. It will alter tests if you let it. It will produce code that looks plausible and is structurally wrong.

So I do not rely on AI for architecture. I use it for:

  • Drafting.
  • Criticism.
  • Research assistance.
  • Code completion.
  • Small implementation slices.
  • Test generation. Comparing alternative designs.
  • Finding contradictions.

The responsibility for the system design remains mine. The most important rule is that the AI must be boxed in. Detailed specifications, small tasks, tests before code, and regular full test runs are not optional. I currently have more than 6000 tests in the CTest suite, and each reference engine’s regression suite is treated as a major test target.

Another practical tip: read the AI’s reasoning while it is working, when the tool exposes it. You can often catch the wrong turn before it becomes a disaster.

My trust in AI went down at first, because I saw how badly it could fail. Then it went back up, but in a different way. I no longer trust it as an engineer. I trust it as a tool that can be very productive inside a controlled process.

You have mentioned using multiple AI agents, and you also maintain a separate ScratchBird-ai repository. How are these pieces organized in practice? Are agents specialized by task, working iteratively, or layered in some form of orchestration? And how do you prevent fragmentation?

The ScratchBird-ai repository is not the AI that writes the code, and it is not just a set of hooks to outside APIs. It is a full MCP layer so that an AI can use the database as a tool. In other words, it is about making ScratchBird accessible to AI systems in a structured way. The AI can query, store, retrieve, and operate through the database instead of treating the database as just an external blob of state. That also helped me test vector indexes and AI-oriented access patterns.

For the development process itself, I use multiple models in different roles. One model may draft, another may criticize, another may rewrite, another may test, and another may compare against specifications. I try not to let a single model both create and approve its own work. Fragmentation is controlled through specifications, workplans, tests, and traceability. If it is not in the specification, the AI should not invent it. If implementation changes the design, the specification must be updated. If tests fail, the implementation is wrong until proven otherwise.

All specifications and code is auditable - I have the specifications updated to contain the path/file/search key for every completed specification - the specification tells you something is finished, you can see for yourself, walk the code and double check everything. This is also good for the AI to use to find the materials it needs. Also, specifications need to be compared against once another -this can take days and must be addressed one specification at a time. You have to compare every single specification and index against every other specification and index to ensure that there is no specification and in turn code drift.

With AI generating or modifying significant parts of the system, how do you maintain architectural coherence and correctness? What mechanisms do you rely on to validate AI-produced code and ensure it aligns with your intended design?

The main mechanism is that architecture is not allowed to live only in my head or in a chat window. It has to be written down. ScratchBird is driven by specifications, workplans, conformance tests, implementation traces, and regression tests. The more complex the subsystem, the more explicit the specification needs to be. The process is roughly:

1. Define the behavior in the specification.

2. Identify the inputs, outputs, error cases, diagnostics, metrics, and invalid states.

3. Write or update tests before trusting implementation changes.

4. Give the AI a small bounded task.

5. Have another model review the result against the specification.

6. Run targeted tests during development and full regression runs regularly.

7. If implementation and specification disagree, stop and reconcile them.

This process is a round robin approach with each stage possibly going through multiple rounds of cross checking/review/updates by all the different ai models.

I also try to avoid giving AI large, vague tasks like “refactor the engine.” That is how you get corruption. Instead, the task has to be something like “implement this one diagnostic vector field according to this section and do not touch anything else.” The tests are important, but tests alone are not enough. AI can write bad tests too. That is why the specifications matter so much. The specification is the thing the test and implementation are both judged against.

The other mechanism is adversarial review. I ask models to attack the work, not praise it. A model that is rewarded for finding contradictions is much more useful than a model that is trying to be agreeable.

Based on your experience, where does AI genuinely help when building a database engine, and where does it fall short today? What advances would make a meaningful difference?

AI helps most when the problem is bounded. It is good at generating boilerplate, comparing approaches, finding missing cases, writing first-pass tests, summarizing reference material, and helping you explore designs. It is also useful as a critic, especially if you use multiple models and make them disagree with each other. Where it falls short is ownership.

A database engine is a large, complex, detailed system. Correctness depends on many small rules interacting properly: transactions, visibility, storage, recovery, memory, indexes, diagnostics, wire protocols, security, and compatibility behavior. AI does not naturally maintain that kind of architectural coherence over time.

It is like a junior developer who is brilliant, lazy, forgetful, and very good at sounding confident. That is useful if you supervise it. It is dangerous if you believe everything it says.

Never use only one model. Different models make different mistakes. Their inference patterns differ, and that can be used to your advantage.

I see AI as another layer of tooling. Machine language gave way to high-level languages. High-level languages gained IDEs, refactoring tools, static analyzers, and test frameworks. AI is another layer on top of that. If you are a developer, you need to learn how to use it. But “vibe coding” is not engineering. It is often a non-coder believing the lies the AI is feeding them.

The advances I want are practical:

  • Better long-term memory with verifiable source grounding.
  • Better ability to obey negative constraints.
  • Stronger test-generation discipline.
  • Model-level honesty about uncertainty.
  • Better tooling for cross-checking code against specifications.
  • Agents that can maintain traceability without inventing completion.
  • Better ways to compare one model’s work against another’s

The biggest improvement would be AI that can say, “I do not know,” and actually stop.

After everything you have explored with ScratchBird, architecture, AI, and system design, what has surprised you the most personally in this process?

What surprised me most was how easy parts of it became once I understood the limitations. That does not mean the work is easy. Database engines are hard. Distributed systems are hard. Compatibility layers are hard. But the process became manageable when I stopped trying to make AI act like a senior engineer and started treating it like a tool that needs structure. I designed around small elements. Each piece has a specific task. Small tasks build into larger ones. That is old engineering advice, but it matters even more with AI. Once I accepted that, the workflow started to feel like having a team of developers available without meetings, approvals, or a lot of the overhead that slows projects down.You still need judgment. You still need discipline. You still need tests. You still need to understand what you are building. But if you provide those things, AI can help move very quickly.

Notes: The source-available donor and reference systems I studied include: Apache Ignite, Cassandra, ClickHouse, CockroachDB, Dolt, DuckDB, Firebird, FoundationDB, immudb, InfluxDB, MariaDB, Milvus, MongoDB, MySQL, Neo4j, OpenSearch, PostgreSQL, Redis, SQLite, TiDB, TiKV, Vitess, XTDB, and YugabyteDB

Conway's Law

This law suggests that the technical boundaries of a system will reflect the structure of the organisation. It is commonly referred to when looking at organisation improvements, Conway's Law suggests that if an organisation is structured into many small, disconnected units, the software it produces will be. If an organisation is built more around 'verticals' which are oriented around features or services, the software systems will also reflect this.

Security Update: April 2026 Maintenance Releases

On 17 April 2026, the Firebird project released maintenance updates for all supported branches (5.0.4, 4.0.7 and 3.0.14). In addition to routine fixes and improvements, these releases addressed nine Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs).

While this number may seem unusually high for Firebird, it reflects a focused security effort rather than a decline in quality. A sponsor-backed bug bounty initiative, likely supported by AI-assisted analysis, led to a more systematic search for vulnerabilities and the discovery of issues that might otherwise have remained unnoticed.

This development mirrors a broader industry trend. Advances in large language models are making vulnerability discovery faster and more accessible, affecting both open-source and proprietary software. As a result, more vulnerabilities are being identified across the ecosystem, and exploit development is becoming increasingly sophisticated.

Users are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the latest maintenance releases when feasible. Although many of the reported vulnerabilities require specific conditions or prior access to the server, and overall risk remains relatively low, regular updates are becoming increasingly important in this evolving security landscape.

Awesome Firebird on GitHub

Finding the right Firebird-related library, driver, administration tool or learning resource can sometimes be a challenge. To make this easier, the Firebird Project maintains an official Awesome Firebird repository on GitHub, a curated collection of community projects, tools, drivers, client libraries, documentation, articles and other useful resources.

Like all "awesome" lists, its value depends on contributions from the community. If you know of a Firebird-related project or resource that deserves wider recognition, please help keep the list up to date. The easiest way is to submit a pull request to the GitHub repository. If GitHub is not your preferred way of contributing, simply send us an email with the details—we will be happy to review your suggestion and add it to the list if appropriate.

The Second-System Effect

The second is the most dangerous system a man ever designs.

Frederick P. Brooks Jr.

The Second-System Effect describes the tendency for a successful first system to be followed by an over-engineered or bloated second system. Frederick P. Brooks Jr. introduced the phrase in The Mythical Man-Month, where he argued that a first system is often built conservatively because its designers are still learning and proceed with restraint.

After that initial success, deferred ideas and increased confidence can make the second system more ambitious. This is relevant to rewrites, major version 2 projects and platform rebuilds: a replacement system can be useful when the first version has taught the team what the real problem is, but it can also become harder to build, understand and maintain if it attempts to solve too many speculative future needs at once.

Brooks used IBM’s OS/360 as a key example of the Second-System Effect in The Mythical Man-Month, contrasting its ambitious scope with earlier, simpler IBM operating systems.

Every PROJECT begins with an idea, but it is remembered because of the people who carried it forward.

Toolbox: RazorSQL

RazorSQL, developed by Richardson Software LLC, is a cross-platform SQL editor, database browser, and database administration tool designed to work with dozens of database systems through JDBC, and ODBC connections. Rather than focusing on a single database engine, RazorSQL aims to provide a consistent working environment for developers, database administrators, and analysts who regularly work across multiple database platforms.

RazorSQL version 10.6.8 (64-bit Linux edition) was used for this review.

RazorSQL requires Java 1.8 or later and currently ships with an embedded Java 17 runtime, eliminating the need for a separate Java installation. The software is available as ZIP archives (or DMG images on macOS) for 32-bit and 64-bit Windows, Linux, macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon), and various Unix platforms, including Solaris. Traditional executable installers are also provided for Windows. RazorSQL is commercial software licensed on a per-user basis and operates as a fully functional 30-day trial without a valid license.

Out of the box, RazorSQL supports approximately 50 database systems, with additional databases accessible through JDBC drivers. The distribution includes native JDBC drivers for 23 database platforms, including Jaybird 4.0.3 for Firebird, as well as a Universal JDBC driver. Users are not restricted to the bundled drivers and can easily configure alternative or newer driver versions when required.

An interesting option is the RazorSQL JDBC Bridge, which allows database access without a direct client-to-database connection. The bridge is implemented as a JavaServer Page (JSP) application that can be deployed to any Java Servlet container. Once configured, RazorSQL communicates with the bridge, which in turn connects to the target database. This architecture can be useful in environments where direct database connectivity is restricted by network or security policies.

Additionally, RazorSQL includes a dedicated Local Database based on the embedded HSQLDB engine. It can be used as a personal workspace for storing tables copied from connected databases. Using the Copy to Local Database feature, users can transfer table definitions alone or complete tables with their data, making the Local Database useful for offline analysis, experimentation, and data comparison.

Defining a Firebird connection is straightforward and intuitive, especially if you are used to working with the Jaybird driver. The only difficulty is defining specific parameters, as RazorSQL only defines encoding and roleName. So if you need to set other parameters (e.g. sessionTimeZone), you will need to consult the driver documentation.

The user interface is functional rather than elegant, with a familiar design that should feel immediately comfortable to most database professionals. The application uses a traditional desktop window with menus and toolbars, while the main workspace is organized as a collection of tabbed panels that occupy the entire client area.

Most panels are associated with a database connection and provide three primary work areas: a navigation tree containing database objects, an SQL editor, and query result displays. Another type of panel provides only a text editor and is intended primarily for working with the source code of procedures, triggers, and other database objects, although it can also be used for external SQL scripts and text files.

While the overall layout is fixed, individual workspace components can be shown or hidden as needed. The object browser, SQL editor, and query output areas can be shown or hidden as needed. The object browser, SQL editor, and query output areas can be enabled or disabled independently, allowing users to adapt the workspace to the task at hand without changing its fundamental structure.

RazorSQL is designed primarily as a multi-database tool, and this philosophy is reflected throughout the application. Its features, user interface, and workflows are built around supporting a wide range of database platforms rather than maximizing integration with any single one. Unlike some competing products that rely on database-specific plugins or dedicated management panels, RazorSQL adopts a unified approach based on a common interface and a consistent set of tools across all supported database systems.

The downside of this broad and consistent approach is that support for database-specific functionality is frequently limited to what can be exposed through standard JDBC mechanisms. Consequently, some Firebird-specific features are absent or less convenient than in dedicated Firebird administration tools.

That is certainly bad for traditional database administration or development tool, but RazorSQL is clearly intended as a broader DevOps-oriented environment. While it provides solid support for common database tasks, such as executing SQL statements and scripts, analyzing query results, importing and exporting data, performing minor schema modifications, managing backups, and examining execution plans, a significant portion of its value lies in automation and auxiliary capabilities such as script development and execution across multiple languages, (S)FTP file transfer, or general file management. In practice, database work represents only part of its overall functionality.

As a result, RazorSQL often feels less like a dedicated database client and more like a general database workstation that brings together numerous administrative and development tools within a single environment.

Conclusion

RazorSQL makes the most sense in heterogeneous environments where multiple database systems are used alongside a variety of operational tasks. In such contexts, its unified approach and integrated toolset can provide a practical advantage, even if it does not excel in any single area.

Tesler’s Law (of Conservation of Complexity)

This law states that there is a certain amount of complexity in a system which cannot be reduced.

Some complexity in a system is 'inadvertent'. It is a consequence of poor structure, mistakes, or just bad modeling of a problem to solve. Inadvertent complexity can be reduced (or eliminated). However, some complexity is 'intrinsic' as a consequence of the complexity inherent in the problem being solved. This complexity can be moved, but not eliminated.

One interesting element to this law is the suggestion that even by simplifying the entire system, the intrinsic complexity is not reduced, it is moved to the user, who must behave in a more complex way.

Answers to your questions

Documentation is said to be a collection of answers to unspoken questions. If you ask a search engine, it will answer you with a link to a document that (hopefully) contains the answer. There are documents, forums and entire systems like Stack Overflow that consisting only of questions and answers. And now an army of AIs is starting to chase us to answer our questions. Questions and answers cannot be avoided, there is no hiding place.

However, amidst the sea of routine questions and responses, there lie truly captivating inquiries and answers, like hidden treasures. Our commitment is to regularly present you with a curated collection of these precious gems.

This time about:

  • Size of NULL columns
  • Lesson about Classic server and per-connection cache size
  • Table structure for efficient storage

Size of NULL columns

korkless asked:

Is there some formula to know (even if not exactly) how much space is used by a null field and by a column of nulls (i have same columns where only < 1% of the fields are not null

Ann W. Harrison answers:

In memory, a record consists of a record header, one bit for each field to represent its null state then rounded up the nearest multiple of eight, plus the declared size of each field. Fields with the null bit set are filled with zeros for numeric and date types, and spaces (IIRC) for character and varchar fields.

Before begin written to disk, the whole record undergoes run length compression using a byte counter. So a string of null numbers turns into a byte of length and a byte of zero. Nulls take just as much (or as little) space as the same field with a value of 0 or ''.

Lesson about Classic server and per-connection cache size

svanderclock asked:

I discovered that when I setup the page buffers on the isc_attach_database (with isc_dpb_num_buffers) then the parameter is used ONLY IF the database page buffers was explicity set to 0 at the database level !

But if I set a page buffer on the connection (for exemple because i will do intensive update), it’s mean i want this page buffer in any case, even if in the database it’s was set to a lower value (that i imagine fit the normal usage of the database).

Ivan Prenosil answers:

Yes, number of pages set by database administrator has higher precedence than arbitrary value set during connect, otherwise irresponsible users could easily cause fb server to run out of virtual space.

Table structure for efficient storage

Daniel L. Miller asked:

Having just read the thread on CHAR vs SMALLINT for storing a single byte

Does the order/sequence of columns in a table make a difference in storage? I.e., is a table of CHAR(1), CHAR(1), CHAR(1), CHAR(1), SMALLINT, VARCHAR(50) stored differently than CHAR(1), SMALLINT, CHAR(1), VARCHAR(50), CHAR(1), CHAR(1)?

Ann W. Harrison answers:

Yes it is, but it’s not worth worrying about. There are two considerations: the number of pad bytes introduced to maintain field alignment in the record buffer and the effect of run-length compression.

The record buffer is constructed so fields are aligned on their natural boundaries. If you’ve got a CHAR(1) field followed by an int, Firebird with put in three pad bytes so the int starts on a four-byte boundary. It’s more efficient to store fields based on their alignment - highest alignment first. If you don’t like the way that looks when you do a SELECT *, use the position attribute on the fields to define the output field order.

Run-length compression is data dependent - runs of identical bytes are compressed to a length byte and a data byte, so the amount of storage used will vary with the values stored. Note that the compression is byte-wise. Two-byte characters do not compress well. The biggest gain from compression is the elimination of trailing spaces in long strings and spaces or zeros in null fields. Putting nullable fields together helps compression especially if you separate character fields from dates and number that are zero filled. Varchar fields are both numbers and characters, so they’re less compressible when they’re null than CHAR. But they’re also much easier to work with.

Disks are cheap.
