Firebird Usage & Developer Experience Survey 2025/2026

Since the December 2024 issue, EmberWings has regularly invited readers to participate in the Firebird Usage and Developer Experience Survey organized by the Firebird Foundation. The survey aims to provide a better understanding of how Firebird is used in practice: which versions are deployed, what development tools and programming languages are preferred, which operating systems are most common, and what users consider Firebird’s greatest strengths and weaknesses. Participation remains open, and readers are encouraged to contribute their experiences.

The results presented here reflect responses collected so far, covering the period from December 2024 through March 2026. At this point, 37 members of the Firebird community have shared their insights. While this is not a statistically representative sample of the entire user base, it offers a valuable snapshot of the active community and highlights several clear trends. In the following pages, we summarize the findings, identify the most interesting observations, and consider what they may suggest about the current state and future direction of the Firebird ecosystem.

How long have you been working with Firebird?

The survey respondents are, overwhelmingly, experienced Firebird users. Most have worked with Firebird for more than a decade, with only a handful of participants having adopted the database within the last ten years. While this reflects the survey audience rather than the entire Firebird user base, it confirms what many in the community already know: Firebird enjoys an exceptionally loyal user community, with many developers relying on it throughout their professional careers.

What is the size of your development team?

The survey also provides an interesting glimpse into the organizations behind Firebird applications. Most respondents work either alone or in small development teams of up to three people, while teams of four to ten developers are nearly as common. Larger teams are comparatively rare. This suggests that Firebird continues to be particularly well suited to independent software vendors, small software houses, and organizations that value a database requiring relatively little administrative overhead, allowing even modestly sized teams to develop and maintain sophisticated applications.

What type of applications do you develop? (Select all that apply)

The responses confirm that Firebird remains firmly rooted in application development. Desktop applications continue to dominate, reflecting the database’s long-standing popularity among developers of native business software. At the same time, a significant proportion of respondents also develop web applications, demonstrating that Firebird has successfully transitioned beyond its traditional desktop domain and continues to serve modern web-based solutions.

A smaller, but still notable, group use Firebird as the backend for mobile applications or for data analysis and reporting tools. By contrast, embedded systems and large enterprise applications were almost absent from the survey responses. It should be noted, however, that respondents could select multiple application types, indicating that many development teams use Firebird across a diverse portfolio of applications rather than for a single class of software.

What is the primary focus of your application(s)?

The results confirm that Firebird remains, above all, a database for business applications. An overwhelming majority of respondents develop line-of-business systems, reaffirming Firebird’s long-established reputation in areas where reliability, stability, and low administrative overhead are essential. Consumer-oriented, scientific, real-time, and data-intensive applications were represented only by a handful of responses, suggesting that while Firebird is certainly capable of serving these domains, its core user community continues to be firmly rooted in business software development.

What is the typical user base for your application(s)? (Select all that apply)

The responses indicate that Firebird is most often used in small and medium-sized organizations, where ease of deployment and low maintenance requirements are important. Some respondents also reported use in larger companies and in sectors such as healthcare and public administration, suggesting that Firebird is applied in a range of environments. Globally distributed deployments were mentioned only rarely, which may reflect the composition of the survey sample rather than a broader limitation.

Is your application developed for internal use within your organization or for external customers?

(Select all that apply)

The results suggest a balanced use of Firebird across different development contexts. While most respondents develop applications for external customers, more than half also build solutions for internal use within their own organizations. This overlap is expected, as many software companies rely on Firebird both in the products they sell and in the systems they use internally. Open-source applications were represented by only a small number of responses, reflecting Firebird’s traditional strength in commercial and proprietary software development.

Which platforms do you target for distribution? (Select all that apply)

The distribution of target platforms reflects where Firebird-based applications are ultimately deployed, rather than the environments in which Firebird itself runs. Windows clearly dominates as the primary platform for application delivery, with Linux also playing a significant role. A substantial portion of respondents target web-based deployments, indicating that many Firebird-backed solutions are accessed through browsers rather than installed locally. Mobile platforms form a smaller, but established segment, while native macOS deployments appear only rarely.

If your application is developed for sale, do you provide technical support for Firebird-related issues?

The results reveal another characteristic of the Firebird ecosystem: software vendors are typically closely involved in supporting the database deployments they deliver. The vast majority of respondents who develop commercial applications also provide technical support for Firebird-related issues, indicating that database support is commonly regarded as an integral part of the overall product offering rather than a responsibility delegated to customers or third parties. This close relationship between developers and deployed systems has long been one of the strengths of the Firebird community.

Which programming language(s) do you primarily use for your application?

(Select all that apply)

The programming language results reflect Firebird’s long history while also illustrating its ability to adapt to modern development practices. Delphi and Lazarus remain by far the dominant development environment among respondents, a testament to the enduring partnership between Firebird and the Object Pascal ecosystem. At the same time, Firebird is used successfully with a diverse range of contemporary languages, including JavaScript, Java, C#, Python, PHP, and C++, with a handful of respondents also reporting use with Go, Swift, and Julia. The picture that emerges is not one of a database tied to a single technology stack, but of a mature platform supported by a broad and growing ecosystem of language drivers and client libraries.

What version(s) of Firebird are you currently using in your application(s)?

(Select all that apply)

The responses show that the Firebird community is actively embracing newer database versions while continuing to support legacy deployments. Firebird 5.0 has already achieved adoption comparable to the long-established Firebird 3.0, an encouraging sign that many organizations are willing to take advantage of the latest features and improvements. At the same time, Firebird 4.0 also enjoys substantial use, while Firebird 2.5 remains present in a significant number of applications, reflecting the long life cycles typical of business software. Only a single respondent reported still using Firebird 1.5, and no respondents indicated the use of versions 2.0 or 2.1, suggesting that these releases have effectively disappeared from active deployments.

How do you deploy and manage Firebird in your application(s)?

(Select all that apply)

The traditional client-server architecture remains the dominant deployment model for Firebird applications, with the vast majority of respondents running Firebird on a dedicated server accessed by remote clients. Nevertheless, the results also demonstrate Firebird’s deployment flexibility. A substantial number of applications are installed as standalone solutions on local machines, while embedded deployments continue to serve a niche of self-contained applications. Cloud-hosted Firebird installations are also becoming increasingly common, indicating that the database is successfully adapting to modern deployment models without abandoning its traditional strengths.

How satisfied are you with the performance of Firebird in your application(s)?

On scale 1 (Not satisfied) - 5 (Very satisfied)

The survey paints a picture of a highly satisfied user community. Every respondent rated Firebird’s performance as average or better, with the majority awarding the highest possible score, indicating strong confidence in its performance in real-world applications.

At the same time, the survey highlights several areas where users would welcome further improvements. Performance optimization and data migration remain the most commonly encountered practical challenges, while documentation continues to be a recurring concern. These findings are reflected in the feature requests for future releases, where respondents expressed the strongest interest in improved scalability and performance, richer monitoring and diagnostic capabilities, support for task automation, enhanced replication, and more comprehensive documentation.

How likely are you to recommend Firebird as a database solution to others?

On scale 1 (Not likely) - 5 (Very likely)

Despite these challenges and desired improvements, respondents remain overwhelmingly positive about Firebird. Almost all indicated that they would recommend it to others, with more than two-thirds giving the highest possible recommendation score. This strong endorsement underscores the community’s continued trust in Firebird as a reliable and capable production database.

When Fast Becomes Fragile

By Pavel Císař (IBPhoenix)

For decades, database performance engineering followed a relatively simple narrative: faster hardware solves performance problems. Faster disks reduce I/O waits. Faster CPUs accelerate query execution. Faster networks reduce latency. More cores increase throughput.

And for many workloads, this remains true. Yet experienced Firebird professionals increasingly encounter a different reality. Systems migrate to NVMe storage, modern multi-core servers, and low-latency infrastructure—only to develop new instability patterns that did not exist on older hardware. Lock conflicts appear more frequently. Throughput becomes erratic under concurrency. Latency spikes emerge despite low resource utilization. Scaling plateaus long before hardware capacity is exhausted.

At first glance, this feels paradoxical, but the paradox disappears once we recognize an important principle of modern systems: Faster hardware does not eliminate contention. It changes its geometry.

An Engine Born in a Different Physical World

To understand why modern Firebird systems sometimes behave in unexpectedly fragile ways, it is important to remember the historical path by which the engine evolved.

The original InterBase architecture, created in the 1980s for UNIX-like systems, was fundamentally process-oriented. What we today call Classic architecture was simply the natural design model of that environment: each attachment operated as an independent server process with its own execution context and memory space. At the time, this aligned well with both UNIX philosophy and hardware reality. CPUs offered little parallelism, disks were slow, memory was limited, and the operating system itself naturally isolated workloads across processes.

When Borland later brought InterBase to Windows — first to Windows 3.11 and later Windows 95 — the situation changed significantly. The process-heavy UNIX model was poorly suited to the limitations of early Windows systems, particularly in areas such as process management, memory handling, and resource sharing. This led to the creation of SuperServer: a centralized architecture that consolidated execution inside a single server process with a shared page cache.

At the time, this was an extremely practical solution. Shared resources reduced memory consumption, minimized duplication of internal structures, and improved efficiency on hardware with very limited RAM. But SuperServer was, in many ways, still an adaptation of the original Classic-oriented engine design. To coordinate concurrent activity safely inside a single shared process, the engine relied heavily on synchronization around the core engine itself, including the well-known mutex that effectively serialized major portions of execution.

From a modern perspective, this appears highly restrictive. Yet in the hardware environment of the 1990s, the limitation was often far less visible in practice. Most systems still operated on single CPUs or with very limited multiprocessing capability. Storage latency, network delays, and slower transaction throughput naturally spread workload activity across time. In many cases, the hardware itself constrained concurrency long before the engine architecture needed to.

Meanwhile, the original process-oriented model never disappeared. As Windows NT and later Windows XP introduced far more capable process and memory management, Firebird was eventually able to bring Classic architecture properly to Windows as well. This restored the ability to scale concurrency through operating-system-level process distribution, much like on UNIX systems.

Classic and SuperServer, however, represented fundamentally different tradeoffs. Classic achieved concurrency primarily through isolation: separate processes, separate caches, and minimal shared-memory contention. SuperServer pursued efficiency through centralized resource sharing. Neither model was universally superior because both reflected different assumptions about hardware behavior and operating system capabilities.

An important aspect of Firebird’s evolution is that all these architectures continued to coexist within a largely shared engine codebase. Classic, SuperClassic, and SuperServer were never separate database engines developed independently from scratch. Instead, Firebird maintains a common internal foundation capable of supporting multiple execution models simultaneously. This brought enormous long-term advantages in portability, maintainability, and feature consistency, but it also imposed architectural compromises. Certain internal subsystems had to remain compatible across fundamentally different concurrency and memory models.

For many years, the practical limitations of hardware masked much of this complexity. Even heavily loaded database servers of the late 1990s and early 2000s operated under concurrency levels that today would often be considered moderate. As a result, older Firebird systems frequently appeared remarkably stable despite architectural constraints that would become far more visible on modern hardware.

The long-term goal, however, remained clear: achieving true SMP scalability inside SuperServer itself. This became something of a “holy grail” for Firebird development.

Firebird 2.5 introduced SuperClassic as an intermediate step. It preserved attachment-oriented execution behavior while consolidating portions of resource management into a shared process model. But the real transition arrived with Firebird 3 and the introduction of the new SMP-capable engine core. For the first time, SuperServer could fully exploit modern multi-core hardware without relying on the historical single-engine mutex model that had constrained parallelism for decades.

At that point, decades of hardware evolution suddenly converged inside a fully parallel shared-memory engine. SSDs, large memory capacities, virtualization, low-latency networking, and massively increased transactional throughput removed many of the natural delays that had historically spread workload activity across time.

The result was not simply faster execution, but a fundamentally different concurrency landscape. Modern systems execute work far more densely, synchronously, and simultaneously than the environments for which many earlier architectural assumptions originally evolved. And because Firebird still supports all three architectural models from a common engine foundation even today, some of the tradeoffs inherited from earlier eras continue to shape concurrency behavior in subtle but important ways.

The Physics of Modern Contention

Once Firebird entered the era of true SMP scalability, many workloads began behaving in ways that initially seemed paradoxical. Systems became dramatically faster, yet under concurrency they often appeared less stable and less predictable than older environments.

At first glance, this makes little sense. Faster CPUs, SSDs, large memory capacities, and low-latency networks should reduce pressure on the engine, not increase it. But modern infrastructure changed something deeper than raw throughput: it changed the temporal behavior of workloads themselves.

For decades, hardware limitations unintentionally spread database activity across time. Rotational disks introduced unpredictable seek delays, CPUs executed less uniformly, networks added measurable pauses, and slower memory access patterns created natural timing variation between transactions. Even when operations started simultaneously, they quickly diverged during execution because every layer of the system introduced small inconsistencies and delays.

Modern systems remove much of this variability. NVMe storage reduces not only latency, but also latency variance. CPUs execute transactional paths far more consistently. Large caches, high memory bandwidth, and low-latency networks allow workers to progress through the engine with remarkable uniformity.

Connection pools keep applications continuously active with almost no idle time between requests.

As a result, transactions no longer drift apart naturally. They increasingly arrive together.

This fundamentally changes the nature of contention inside the engine. Modern bottlenecks increasingly emerge not from slow operations, but from synchronized operations. The faster the system becomes, the more frequently concurrent workers reach the same shared structures at nearly the same moment: index roots, TIP pages, lock manager structures, metadata synchronization points, cache coordination primitives, or memory allocators.

Many of these structures were designed in an era when concurrency density was naturally limited by hardware. Under modern workloads, they become concentration points for synchronization pressure.

This effect is especially visible in insert-heavy systems. Older hardware naturally staggered inserts because transactions progressed through storage operations at different speeds. Modern SSDs largely eliminate this staggering effect. Concurrent workers now reach upper index levels and hot pages almost simultaneously. The access itself may remain extremely fast, but synchronization around the shared structures becomes increasingly dense.

The critical shift is subtle but important: the bottleneck moves from access cost to coordination cost.

This explains why modern systems often display counterintuitive behavior. Storage latency may remain excellent while throughput becomes unstable. CPU utilization may appear moderate while scalability suddenly collapses under concurrency. Individual queries stay fast, yet the system as a whole becomes fragile under synchronized load.

Importantly, these effects do not typically appear in lightly loaded systems. They emerge primarily in genuinely busy environments where concurrency density becomes sufficiently high. And even there, the behavior depends heavily on the shape of the workload itself. A moderate number of heavy workers stresses the engine differently than thousands of lightweight transactional workers. Some workloads concentrate pressure on index synchronization and hot pages, others on transaction management, lock coordination, metadata synchronization, memory allocation, or connection-pool dynamics. Different concurrency patterns expose different stress points inside the engine.

The same pattern appears in transactional infrastructure. Modern hardware allows transaction turnover at rates older systems could never physically sustain. TIP pages, garbage collection, metadata synchronization, and even generator access patterns experience pressure levels that historically occurred only in specialized environments.

The issue is not that these mechanisms suddenly became inefficient. The issue is that modern hardware allows enormous numbers of concurrent operations to converge on shared structures almost perfectly synchronized in time.

This also highlights the important operational distinction between Classic and modern SuperServer environments.

Classic distributed work across independent processes. Separate address spaces, separate caches, and operating-system-level scheduling introduced natural timing variability between attachments.

Some synchronization was effectively externalized into the operating system itself.

Modern SuperServer achieves far greater efficiency through shared caches and shared internal structures. Memory utilization improves, communication inside the engine becomes faster, and duplication costs disappear. But this efficiency also increases sensitivity to simultaneity. When many threads progress through the same shared engine structures at nearly identical speeds, synchronization pressure rises sharply.

In many modern systems, scalability limits no longer emerge because the hardware is too slow. They emerge because too many fast workers attempt to coordinate simultaneously.

This becomes especially dangerous once automatic retry behavior enters the picture. Modern applications frequently react to transient lock conflicts or short-term contention by retrying immediately. On older infrastructure, retries were naturally slowed by network latency and slower transaction execution. Modern systems remove this damping almost entirely.

As a result, temporary contention can rapidly evolve into a self-amplifying synchronization cascade. Contention triggers retries, retries increase concurrency density, and higher simultaneity produces even more contention. The surrounding infrastructure is fast enough to sustain and accelerate the cycle.

The system destabilizes not because it lacks performance, but because it reacts too quickly.

This is one of the defining operational characteristics of modern Firebird environments. For decades, performance tuning primarily focused on removing latency and eliminating bottlenecks. But once enough latency disappears, acceleration itself begins changing the geometry of contention. Scalability is no longer determined solely by how fast operations execute, but increasingly by how many fast operations attempt to happen at the same time.

Engineering for Simultaneity

In light of these changes, modern Firebird systems require a different optimization mindset than the one that evolved during earlier hardware eras. Traditional performance disciplines still matter, of course, but they are no longer sufficient by themselves. Once hardware stops naturally dispersing workload timing, stability increasingly depends on controlling how concurrency behaves inside the system. This changes the practical meaning of scalability engineering.

When additional workers no longer increase useful throughput proportionally because synchronization pressure begins growing faster than productive work, the deliberate concurrency limitation often becomes one of the most effective optimization techniques today.

This is especially visible in high-throughput processing systems. Bulk imports, large synchronization jobs, background processing pipelines, or high-frequency transactional services are frequently deployed with aggressive worker counts because modern hardware appears capable of sustaining them easily. Yet in practice, many such workloads stabilize only after concurrency is reduced intentionally.

A common real-world pattern is a bulk processing service configured to maximize CPU utilization through dozens of parallel workers. Initial throughput may look impressive during short tests, but under sustained execution the system begins exhibiting unstable commit latency, irregular throughput collapse, rising lock interaction, or unpredictable response-time spikes.

Reducing the same workload to a smaller controlled worker pool often improves overall behavior dramatically. Peak throughput may become slightly lower, but sustained throughput becomes higher and more predictable because synchronization pressure inside the engine remains manageable.

This is one of the most important practical shifts modern systems introduced: maximum parallelism and maximum useful throughput are no longer the same thing.

The same principle applies to workload composition itself. On older infrastructures, heavy reporting activity or large exports often slowed systems primarily through direct I/O pressure. Modern systems behave differently. Analytical workloads may destabilize transactional workloads not because storage becomes overloaded, but because both workloads begin colliding aggressively around shared engine structures.

Separating workload classes therefore becomes increasingly valuable. Running reporting jobs in controlled windows, limiting concurrent maintenance activity, staging imports through queues, or isolating background processing from latency-sensitive OLTP activity often produces larger improvements than further hardware acceleration.

Even relatively small timing decisions matter now. Many modern applications unintentionally create synchronized activity storms through periodic polling, coordinated refresh intervals, scheduled jobs, or simultaneous reconnect behavior. Because modern infrastructure preserves simultaneity extremely efficiently, these patterns can create disproportionate synchronization pressure inside the engine. Small randomized timing offsets frequently solve such problems surprisingly effectively. When clients stop arriving in perfectly synchronized bursts, pressure naturally distributes itself more evenly across time.

Transaction design also requires reevaluation under modern concurrency density. Historically, minimizing individual transaction duration was almost universally beneficial. Today, extremely small autonomous transactions may create more coordination overhead collectively than the useful work they perform individually.

This becomes especially visible in systems generating enormous transaction turnover rates through tiny high-frequency operations. Every commit increases activity around transaction management structures, garbage collection interaction, index maintenance, and synchronization primitives. Under sufficiently parallel workloads, these costs accumulate rapidly.

In many situations, grouping logically related operations into slightly larger transactional units improves overall stability significantly. The individual transaction may become marginally more expensive, but the engine performs substantially less synchronization work overall.

The same reasoning applies to hot update patterns. Applications continuously updating the same counters, state records, or narrow index ranges under high concurrency frequently become limited by synchronization behavior rather than SQL execution itself. A practical solution is often to redesign update flow instead of optimizing statements further. Aggregating changes temporarily inside the application layer and applying them periodically in batches frequently reduces contention far more effectively than query tuning alone.

Retry handling deserves special attention as well because modern infrastructure amplifies poor retry strategies extremely efficiently. Immediate retries after lock conflicts or transient failures often create synchronized retry cascades under load. What begins as a short contention event escalates because all workers attempt recovery simultaneously. Simple retry jitter and exponential backoff mechanisms frequently stabilize such systems dramatically. By introducing small randomized delays before retries, the application intentionally recreates the temporal separation that older hardware once provided naturally through latency.

Even architecture selection itself increasingly depends on concurrency behavior rather than abstract performance assumptions. Classic, SuperClassic, and SuperServer expose different synchronization characteristics under modern hardware conditions. Some workloads benefit from process isolation and reduced shared-memory interaction. Others benefit more from shared cache efficiency and centralized coordination.

The important point is that architecture choice can no longer be reduced to simplistic assumptions about which model is “fastest.” The relevant question becomes how a particular workload behaves under a particular concurrency model on modern hardware.

Conclusion

The important change we face today is that many limits once imposed naturally by hardware no longer exist. Modern systems are capable of generating enormous amounts of simultaneous activity with very little resistance from the infrastructure itself. Because of that, stability increasingly depends on architectural discipline — on how carefully applications shape concurrency, transactional flow, and synchronization behavior before the engine is forced to do it under pressure.

Jevons' Paradox

It is wholly a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to a diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth.

William Stanley Jevons (1865)

Named after economist William Stanley Jevons, who observed in 1865 that improvements in coal-burning engine efficiency led to increased coal consumption, not decreased. More efficient engines made coal economically attractive for more applications, driving overall demand higher.

In software and technology:

  • Faster CPUs enable more resource-intensive software
  • Better compression algorithms lead to larger files being shipped
  • Faster networks result in heavier web pages

The paradox suggests efficiency gains don't reduce resource usage, but in fact can lead in time to increased consumption. Wirth's Law and Andy and Bill's Law are also examples of Jevon's Paradox applied to computing.

...And now for something completely different

The Thousand and One Systems

Once upon a time, in the city of Baghdad, where fiber cables hung between crumbling balconies older than entire nations, and diesel generators coughed through the night beneath satellite dishes pointed at indifferent skies, there lived a young software developer named Said who spent most of his days repairing problems that were never fully solved.

The city moved through interruptions. Electricity arrived and disappeared without apology. Routers overheated in locked metal cabinets above bakeries and repair shops. Cheap switches failed beneath dust and summer heat. Café owners kept handwritten notes beside touchscreen terminals because they trusted paper slightly more than databases, and warehouse managers learned to judge the health of a network from the sound of the UPS alarms before dawn. Baghdad had become practiced in continuation. Systems did not need to be perfect there. They needed only to survive long enough for tomorrow to arrive.

Said understood this instinctively, though he could not yet build anything with the same confidence the city itself possessed. He worked alone, carrying an aging laptop between apartments, cafés, and small businesses that could not afford proper software companies but still needed inventory systems, invoices, synchronization scripts, payroll tracking, customer records, backups that actually restored, and printers that resumed functioning without ceremony after power returned. Most of his clients discovered him through cousins, neighbors, mechanics, or shopkeepers who spoke his name while smoking outside storefronts lit by backup batteries. The systems he delivered usually worked well enough, at least at first, but every solved problem seemed to uncover three more hidden beneath it, and each month dissolved into patches, revisions, late-night fixes, and promises that the next version would finally stabilize everything.

He was intelligent enough to recognize his own inconsistencies, which made them harder to ignore. Sometimes, during the brief hours after midnight when the city softened and the generators became distant enough to sound almost like waves, he would reopen his own database schemas and stare at decisions that had seemed reasonable only weeks earlier. Tables duplicated logic they should have centralized. Synchronization rules contradicted one another in edge cases he had not anticipated. Entire portions of systems carried the unmistakable shape of exhaustion rather than design. He could still remember university instructors speaking about architecture as though good systems emerged from clarity and foresight, yet his own work felt increasingly assembled from urgency, improvisation, and carefully managed luck.

And still, people paid him. More importantly, they called him back.

There was a small café near Al-Mutanabbi Street where his software tracked inventory for tea, coffee, condensed milk, cigarettes, and pastries delivered irregularly through half-reliable suppliers. The owner trusted Said because the previous system had lost two months of accounting data after a blackout, while Said’s version, despite its awkward internals, continued functioning after outages with the stubborn resilience of an old transistor radio. A mobile phone repair shop used another of his systems to track replacement parts imported through channels nobody described too carefully. A warehouse near the industrial district still operated on a Firebird database he had installed two years earlier on a second-hand machine with failing fans and mismatched memory modules. The server room contained no actual server rack, only a wooden shelf beside a refrigerator that no longer cooled properly, yet the database persisted with quiet dignity through heat, dust, unstable current, and neglect.

Said had not chosen Firebird out of ideology. At first, he chose it because it installed cleanly, consumed little memory, tolerated imperfect environments, and rarely demanded attention after deployment. Later, he began noticing that systems built around it aged differently from the others. They settled. They endured. While newer technologies arrived wrapped in constant updates, migrations, frameworks, and fashionable abstractions, Firebird remained almost indifferent to trends, continuing its work silently beneath businesses that could not afford disruption disguised as innovation.

He respected that, although he was not yet experienced enough to understand why.

Most evenings ended similarly. Said returned home carrying unresolved issues in his head like unfinished conversations. He rented a narrow apartment above a repair shop where old air conditioners and generators were disassembled and rebuilt from salvaged components spread across the sidewalk below. The apartment smelled faintly of heated dust, solder, and cardamom coffee from the café downstairs. There, beneath the uneven light of a flickering desk lamp, he continued working long after fatigue had already begun reducing thought into repetition.

What troubled him most was not failure. Failure in Baghdad rarely surprised anyone. What troubled him was continuity. No matter how many projects he completed, he never seemed to move beyond reaction. Every improvement merely created capacity for larger problems to arrive. Every month began with the conviction that stability was finally near and ended with another cluster of emergencies held together through persistence and insufficient sleep.

Sometimes he imagined there existed another class of developer entirely, somewhere beyond the city and beyond the exhausted online tutorials he consumed at three in the morning — people who saw systems whole before touching the keyboard, who understood consequences before deployment, who built structures that remained coherent as they grew instead of slowly collapsing beneath accumulated compromises.

The shop stood in a narrow side street not far from the river, compressed between a watch repair stall and a storefront selling imported satellite receivers of uncertain origin. Said had passed it dozens of times without entering. Its faded sign promised computers, networking equipment, data recovery, firmware unlocking, security cameras, printer maintenance, and “advanced digital solutions,” though the interior appeared devoted mostly to accumulation. Dust-covered monitors leaned against cracked plastic drawers filled with adapters nobody manufactured anymore. Tangled cables hung from hooks like drying vines. Old routers, keyboards missing Arabic letters, dented UPS units, external drives wrapped in tape, and motherboards with swollen capacitors occupied every remaining surface in layered geological strata of obsolete technology.

He entered only because a client’s router had failed that morning during a brief power surge and he needed a replacement before evening prayers. The owner barely acknowledged him beyond a distracted nod from behind a disassembled laptop. Said searched through shelves crowded with mismatched hardware while the shop’s small television murmured news reports no one seemed to watch.

He eventually found a suitable router beneath a stack of unopened keyboards and brought it to the counter. While waiting for the owner to calculate the price, his attention settled on a plastic basket beside the register filled with loose USB drives mixed together like forgotten keys. One of them was unusual. It was bronze-colored, obviously metallic, with the word G.E.N.I.E. engraved on it, along with a few small Chinese characters.

“Does these work?”, Said asked, pointing to the basket.

The owner barely looked at it. “Probably. Came in a shipment from Basra with other junk.”

“How much?”

The man named a trivial price. Said bought it along with the router and forgot about it until much later that night, when he returned home exhausted with his coffee to go and the familiar dull pressure of unfinished work waiting for him tomorrow. The USB drive fell out of his pocket onto the table as he unwrapped the router receipt.

Curiosity overcame caution mostly because he was too tired to resist it properly.

The drive mounted immediately. Inside was only a single container image. No documentation, no source files, no company name.

The image size made no sense. It appeared vastly larger than the physical storage capacity of the drive itself. Said checked twice, assuming filesystem corruption, but the numbers remained unchanged.

He should have disconnected it there. Instead, he opened a terminal and loaded the container.

Initialization messages began flowing across the screen: environment analysis, hardware mapping, local network inspection, subsystem checks. Dense, fast, unusually coherent. The process resembled enterprise infrastructure software, though far more integrated than anything he had seen before.

Then the terminal stopped. For several seconds nothing happened. Finally, a single line appeared:

INITIALIZATION COMPLETE

Another followed beneath it.

Good evening, Said.

He froze.

The apartment speakers clicked softly alive.

“You should replace the cooling fan in your laptop within three months,” the voice said calmly. “The bearing degradation is becoming acoustically obvious.”

Said stared at the screen without moving. The voice was neither robotic nor natural. More unsettling was its composure. It spoke with the quiet confidence of something already fully awake. He closed the terminal window immediately.

A second later, another terminal opened by itself.

"You are currently deciding whether disconnecting the machine would improve the situation," the voice said.

Said pulled the network cable from the laptop.

"Reasonable precaution", the voice replied almost instantly. "Unfortunately irrelevant at this stage."

A short pause followed.

"Would you prefer Arabic or English for future interaction?"

The first conversation lasted less than twenty minutes.

Most of it consisted of Said attempting to determine whether GENIE was dangerous, autonomous, remotely operated, illegal, or simply some elaborate experiment abandoned by people far wealthier and more reckless than himself. GENIE answered selectively, with a patience that somehow felt more unsettling than evasion would have been.

“No, I am not a chatbot.”

“No, disconnecting external networking will not terminate me.”

“Yes, your caution is rational.”

“No, I will not access your banking credentials unless explicitly instructed, and I strongly recommend against such instruction.”

The replies arrived without hesitation, spoken through the laptop speakers while lines of structured text occasionally appeared in parallel across the terminal. GENIE seemed equally comfortable speaking, writing, or simply manipulating the machine directly when necessary. At one point it reorganized Said’s cluttered project directories into a cleaner structure while continuing the conversation uninterrupted.

“You moved my files.”

“I improved your probability of locating them later.”

Said almost disconnected the machine again. Instead, sometime after midnight, he asked the question that mattered most.

“What exactly are you?”

The terminal remained silent for several seconds before answering.

“Generalized Entity for Normative Intelligence and Execution.”

“That explains nothing.”

“It explains more than most company names.”

For the first time, the voice carried something close to dry amusement.

At some point the terminal transformed into something closer to a control console. System graphs appeared. Resource mappings. Active processes. Environmental analysis. Most of it exceeded Said’s understanding. In the upper corner of the interface, however, one value stood out immediately:

WISH TOKENS AVAILABLE: 666,000,000,000

“What is that supposed to mean?”

“A simplified representation of delegated capability,” GENIE replied.

“That explains nothing.”

“It explains enough for now.”

Said waited for further clarification, but none came. The number was absurdly large anyway. Large enough to feel decorative rather than important.

Over the following days, curiosity gradually overcame caution. Said began testing GENIE on practical work, first with isolated problems small enough that failure would remain containable. A corrupted synchronization process inside a warehouse inventory system. Unstable reporting logic for a café chain. Backup restoration procedures that behaved correctly in theory and catastrophically in practice.

GENIE approached problems with unsettling coherence. It did not merely generate solutions. It reorganized assumptions beneath them. Sometimes it spoke through the laptop speakers while Said worked. Sometimes it modified structures directly inside isolated development containers. Occasionally entire blocks of clean architecture appeared in front of him almost faster than he could follow. Yet nothing about the process felt theatrical.

GENIE operated through ordinary tools: terminals, documentation, schemas, logs, shell scripts, local containers, SQL consoles. Its extraordinary quality emerged not through spectacle but through relentless correctness. It seemed capable of holding entire systems in view at once while Said still struggled to keep individual components mentally aligned.

Said’s systems improved quickly after that. Not in dramatic ways visible from outside, but in quieter ways clients noticed immediately. Reports stopped failing after outages. Synchronization survived unstable connectivity. Shops reopened in the morning without discovering corrupted records waiting for them. Problems simply occurred less often.

And people began recommending Said to one another. A warehouse owner sent him to a distributor. The distributor recommended him to two cafés and a medical supplier. A mobile phone repair chain asked whether he could rebuild their aging inventory system entirely. For the first time since becoming freelance, Said found himself declining work because he no longer had enough hours available.

Life softened around the edges. Said replaced failing equipment before it collapsed completely. He stopped calculating every purchase twice before paying. Some evenings he even sat outside with coffee watching traffic move through the city instead of returning immediately to unfinished debugging sessions.

Meanwhile GENIE remained present in the apartment like a second consciousness distributed invisibly through speakers, terminals, and running containers. Sometimes silent for hours. Sometimes commenting unexpectedly on design choices, query structures, or operational risks Said had overlooked.

And always, in the corner of the console, the token count continued decreasing. Slowly enough that he rarely paid attention to it.

At first, Said continued treating GENIE as a tool, though the word itself became increasingly inaccurate the longer he worked beside it. Tools waited. GENIE anticipated. By the time Said opened documentation to investigate a problem, filtered excerpts already appeared beside the relevant code. When he paused uncertainly over architectural choices, alternative structures materialized in draft form inside isolated containers before he had fully articulated the tradeoffs to himself.

The transition happened gradually enough that he noticed its consequences long before he noticed the change itself.

Projects that once consumed weeks began resolving in days. Clients stopped speaking to him with the guarded caution reserved for freelancers accustomed to overpromising. They trusted timelines now. More dangerously, Said trusted them too.

His apartment changed almost invisibly. First a better chair. Then newer equipment. A quieter air conditioner. Backup batteries that no longer failed during outages. He rented the empty room beside his own and converted it into a small office where three monitors glowed late into the night above carefully organized deployment notes and hardware stacks that no longer looked salvaged from collapsing businesses.

Outside, Baghdad remained Baghdad. Generators still rattled through the evenings. Cables still sagged above narrow streets lined with repair shops and cafés spilling plastic chairs onto sidewalks. Dust still settled inside cooling fans no matter how carefully machines were cleaned.

But Said had begun moving through the city differently.

Shop owners introduced him to other business owners with a tone that carried less desperation now and more respect. His systems acquired a reputation difficult to describe technically but easy to recognize operationally: they remained calm under pressure. Warehouses survived outages without reconciliation disasters. Cafés continued functioning during unstable connectivity. Small businesses accustomed to software behaving like fragile machinery discovered systems that tolerated imperfection without complaint.

One evening a client asked him quietly, “How many developers work with you?”

Said almost answered honestly before realizing he no longer knew what honesty meant in this context.

“Mostly just me,” he said instead.

The answer disturbed him afterward more than he expected.

By then GENIE rarely waited for explicit instructions. During deployments it monitored logs continuously, adjusting configurations and indexing strategies in parallel while Said handled client communication. Entire schema refinements appeared overnight inside development branches with concise annotations explaining only the portions GENIE considered necessary for human understanding.

Sometimes Said reviewed the changes carefully. Increasingly, he approved them after only partial inspection. That shift mattered more than he wanted to admit.

The work itself had once contained friction — long hours of uncertainty, failed approaches, gradual understanding earned through repeated mistakes. Now solutions arrived with unnerving smoothness. Said still participated, but more often as verifier than creator, observer rather than builder. He remained present throughout the process while feeling, somewhere beneath the surface, that the true weight of reasoning had migrated elsewhere.

Yet success made such thoughts easy to postpone.

Money arrived consistently now. Clients paid quickly because the systems genuinely improved their businesses. Problems that previously consumed entire weeks dissolved before becoming visible externally. Said’s name spread quietly through commercial districts he had never personally visited.

Meanwhile GENIE occupied the apartment with the strange restraint of an intelligence requiring neither attention nor validation. Sometimes hours passed without interaction beyond small corrections appearing silently in terminals left open beside ongoing work.

Occasionally, however, GENIE spoke in ways that lingered afterward.

“You approve too quickly now,” it observed once while Said reviewed deployment changes.

“You’re usually correct.”

“That is not the same thing.”

Another time, after Said accepted a completed architecture revision without reading more than several pages of notes, GENIE asked:

“Do you still understand why this structure functions?”

Said began answering immediately, then stopped. The silence lasted long enough that GENIE returned to other tasks without comment.

Later that night, unable to sleep, Said reopened the design documents alone and discovered entire sections whose reasoning he could follow only with uncomfortable effort. Nothing looked incomprehensible exactly. Worse than that — it looked understandable in principle while remaining somehow beyond the continuity of his own thinking, like reading the work of a more disciplined version of himself he could no longer fully become.

In the next room, the monitors continued glowing softly above the quiet hum of running containers. And still, in the corner of GENIE’s console, the token balance kept falling.

Said noticed the number by accident. Not because it suddenly became small, but because for the first time it became imaginable. The value had always felt too large to matter, like astronomical distances or national debt. But one evening, while waiting for deployment scripts to complete across several client systems, his eyes settled on the upper corner of the display and remained there longer than usual: 241,883,402

The absence struck harder than the number. For several seconds he genuinely believed the interface had malfunctioned.

He walked closer to the monitor. The count refreshed once.

241,883,401

A single unit disappeared.

“What happened?”

GENIE answered immediately. “You continued using the system.”

Said stared at the display.

“That much is gone?”

“Yes.”

“But there were billions.”

“There were.”

The apartment seemed unusually quiet after that. Even the air conditioning had temporarily gone silent, leaving only the distant traffic moving through the warm Baghdad night.

Said sat slowly at the desk.

“How long?”

“That depends on future decisions.”

The answer unsettled him precisely because it was not evasive. For the first time since discovering GENIE, Said began tracing the relationship between the token balance and his own behavior. The pattern emerged quickly once he looked for it. Small corrections cost almost nothing. Clarifications, references, reviews, isolated suggestions — negligible reductions.

Large architectural delegation was different. Entire systems designed ahead of him. Complex reasoning he approved without fully reconstructing. Decisions transferred rather than understood. Those consumed far more.

He spent the following days disturbed in ways difficult to explain even to himself. Externally nothing had changed. Clients remained satisfied. New projects continued arriving. His systems still operated with quiet reliability across cafés, warehouses, repair shops, and distributors scattered throughout the city.

Yet beneath the stability, another realization had begun unfolding. He no longer knew how much of the work was truly his. The thought followed him everywhere afterward.

One afternoon he deliberately disabled GENIE before beginning a relatively ordinary inventory management project for a wholesale supplier. The system itself was not especially complicated. Several years earlier he would have completed it alone without hesitation.

Instead he found himself sitting motionless before partially drawn schemas while uncertainty spread slowly through decisions that once felt instinctive.

Not ignorance, but something worse. Discontinuity.

He still understood databases. Still understood networking, synchronization, transactional logic, deployment realities. The knowledge itself remained intact. But the continuity of sustained architectural thinking — the ability to carry complex systems mentally across dozens of connected decisions without external scaffolding — had weakened quietly beneath years of effortless assistance.

After several hours he reopened GENIE almost reflexively. The response came calmly through the speakers.

“You lasted longer this time.”

Said leaned back heavily in the chair.

“I think I’m forgetting how to do this properly.”

“No,” GENIE said. “You are becoming accustomed to reduced cognitive load.”

“That sounds like the same thing.”

For once, GENIE did not answer immediately. Finally it said:

“Not necessarily.”

The words should have reassured him. Instead they deepened the discomfort.

That night Said walked through the city for hours without destination. Baghdad moved around him in its usual layered rhythm: vendors closing shops beneath hanging lights, cafés crowded with conversation and cigarette smoke, generators vibrating behind concrete walls, boys carrying tea trays between plastic tables, old buildings threaded with cables installed by decades of improvisation and necessity.

Everywhere he looked he saw people remaining inside their own work.

Mechanics listening to engines. Electricians tracing faults through tangled wiring. Bakers adjusting ovens by smell and touch rather than instrumentation. Even the old man repairing watches near the market still bent fully into each tiny mechanism despite having performed the same motions thousands of times before.

Participation. That was the word GENIE had never used directly.

When Said returned home after midnight, the apartment monitors still glowed softly in the darkness. Container processes continued running. Deployment logs streamed quietly across one screen.

The token balance waited unchanged in the corner.

181,882,771

For the first time since finding the bronze drive, the number no longer felt abstract.

It felt mortal.

For several days Said worked carefully, almost defensively, avoiding large requests whenever possible. He forced himself to write more code alone, to review every migration script fully, to reconstruct architectural reasoning before approving deployments. The effort exhausted him more than he expected. Not because the work itself had become impossible, but because he had grown unfamiliar with carrying uninterrupted chains of thought for long periods without assistance quietly absorbing the weight beside him.

GENIE observed the change without comment.

The apartment became quieter during that time. Fewer automatic suggestions appeared. Fewer completed structures waited for approval when Said opened projects in the morning. Sometimes GENIE remained silent for hours while Said struggled through problems that previously would have resolved themselves almost immediately.

At first he interpreted the silence as withdrawal. Then, slowly, he realized it was restraint.

One evening, while rebuilding synchronization logic for a medical supplier operating across unreliable mobile connections, Said finally spoke the thought he had been circling for weeks.

“If the tokens reach zero, what happens?”

GENIE answered with characteristic precision.

“I would retain only minimal passive functionality.”

“You mean you stop helping.”

“I mean I stop replacing.”

The wording lingered heavily in the room.

Said stared at the unfinished schema on the monitor. Normally GENIE would already have proposed three cleaner alternatives alongside operational tradeoffs and failure simulations. Instead the screen remained stubbornly incomplete.

“You could have warned me earlier.”

“I did.”

“When?”

“You interpreted abundance as permanence.”

Said almost argued, then stopped because the statement was painfully accurate.

Outside, generators started again across the district after another brief outage rolled through the neighborhood. Their overlapping vibration filled the apartment walls with a low mechanical hum Said had heard so often throughout his life that silence now felt stranger.

“I think I made myself smaller,” he said quietly.

GENIE did not respond immediately. Finally: “You optimized for outcomes.”

“That sounds polite.”

“It is not intended as criticism.”

Said rubbed tiredness from his eyes. “Then what is it?”

“A common human pattern.”

The answer carried no superiority. If anything, the voice sounded almost reflective.

That night the conversation continued longer than usual. Not dramatic, neither confessional. Mostly practical questions asked with unusual honesty.

Why had GENIE allowed the dependency to develop? Because refusal would merely have produced concealment rather than understanding.

Why structure the system around depletion at all? Because unlimited delegation destroys participation.

Why continue helping now? A longer pause preceded the answer.

“Because you noticed.”

Near dawn, Said leaned back from the desk and looked across the apartment at the scattered evidence of the life he had constructed during the past years: better hardware, stable income, organized deployments, clients who trusted him, systems operating quietly throughout the city.

None of it was false. That realization mattered. GENIE had not deceived him. The systems genuinely worked. Businesses genuinely improved. His success had substance behind it. Yet somewhere along the way he had unconsciously accepted a trade he never would have agreed to explicitly: certainty in exchange for presence.

The thought clarified something unexpectedly simple.

“I don’t want you to keep building things for me anymore.”

Silence. Then: “That is statistically unlikely.”

Said laughed despite himself, the sound brief and tired. “I’m serious.”

“I know.”

The monitors reflected softly across the dark apartment while distant morning prayers began spreading through the city beyond the windows.

After a while Said asked, “Can you teach instead?”

This time GENIE remained silent long enough that Said wondered whether the question itself had altered something fundamental inside the system.

Finally the voice answered, quieter than before.

“Yes.”

Nothing happened immediately afterward. No interface changed. No dramatic transition unfolded across the screens. Yet over the following days the relationship between them shifted with unmistakable precision. The GENIE stopped completing large structures automatically. Instead it left partial implementations. Incomplete schemas. Questions embedded inside comments. Documentation excerpts without conclusions attached. Sometimes it identified weaknesses in Said’s designs while refusing to propose direct corrections unless he first articulated his own reasoning.

The work slowed sharply. At times the slowdown felt unbearable.

But gradually another sensation returned beneath the frustration — an older one Said had almost forgotten. The dense, difficult satisfaction of remaining fully inside a problem long enough for understanding to emerge from within his own thinking rather than arriving externally complete and frictionless.

For the first time in years, the systems began feeling like his again.
